newsitem.title: USA: Property tax reform delays Vermont Legislature.
newsitem.headline: Property tax reform delays Vermont Legislature.

text.p: Vermont legislators, who at this point in the year would normally be wrapping up business, find themselves scramblng to find a way to fund education.
The Senate education funding bill is in response to the historic Vermont Supreme Court ruling which declared in February that the state's method of funding education is unconstitutional.
The ruling required the Legislature to overhaul the way property taxes are collected and schools are funded throughout the state.

In March, the Vermont House passed a complicated bill which supporters claim is the fairest way to fulfill the Court's mandate. The bill features a two-tiered statewide property tax, a local income tax, and increases in several consumption taxes.

But it is unlikely the House bill, as written, will survive in the Senate. The two most controversial items - the local income tax and the non-residential statewide property tax - are not expected to reaach the Senate floor.

Instead, the Senate approach is likely to be a single statewide property tax rate that is "income sensitive," which means that the amount a property owner pays in taxes will be partially determined by their income.

Debate on the measure is expected to begin next week and if such a measure is approved by the full Senate, it would still have to be reconciled with the House bill. House sentiment against the Senate approach has hardened over the past week.

Only after a joint committee approves a compromise will the bill be ready to be signed into law by Governor Howard Dean. If Dean vetoes the bill, the Legislature may be in session until the snow flies again.
Meanwhile, some legislators are getting restless.
"I hope we wrap this up soon. I've got a farm to run, " Ruth Dwyer (R-Thetford) said. Dwyer owns a cattle and horse farm on the east side of the state.
